title: Demand, Supply and Consumer Behaviour
lines: USAT Economics questions on this topic test whether you know the basic definitions, can tell a shift of a curve from a movement along it, and can do quick elasticity, utility and consumer surplus sums by hand. Expect two or three of the ten Economics questions from here.
## The economic problem

Wants are unlimited but resources are scarce, so every society must choose what to produce, how to produce it and for whom. Choice means sacrifice: the opportunity cost of anything is the next best alternative given up.
- Robbins: economics studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses (scarcity definition).
- Adam Smith called it the science of wealth; Marshall stressed material welfare.
- Microeconomics studies individual units (a consumer, a firm, one market); macroeconomics studies aggregates (national income, the price level).
- Positive statements can be tested by facts; normative statements say what ought to be.

The production possibility curve (PPC) shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can make with its resources and technology. It is bowed outward because opportunity cost rises as more of one good is made. A point inside the curve means unemployed or wasted resources; a point outside is unattainable; better technology or more resources shift the whole curve outward.
## Demand
The law of demand: other things remaining the same (ceteris paribus), quantity demanded falls when price rises. The demand curve slopes downward.
| Change | Effect on the demand curve
| Good's own price | movement along the curve (extension or contraction)
| Income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, population | shift of the whole curve
- Substitutes (tea and coffee): dearer tea raises demand for coffee.
- Complements (cars and petrol): dearer petrol lowers demand for cars.
- Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.
- Exceptions to the law: Giffen goods (a staple inferior good where the income effect outweighs the substitution effect) and Veblen goods (status goods bought because they are dear).
- Derived demand: demand for bricks comes from demand for houses. Joint supply: wheat and straw come together.
## Supply and equilibrium

The law of supply: quantity supplied rises with price. Supply shifts with input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, and the number of firms. Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above it there is a surplus that pushes price down; below it, a shortage that pushes price up.
- Price ceiling (maximum price) below equilibrium causes a shortage.
- Price floor (minimum support price) above equilibrium causes a surplus.
> Qd = 100 − 4P and Qs = 20 + 4P. Find the equilibrium.
> Set 100 − 4P = 20 + 4P, so 80 = 8P and P = Rs 10.
! An increase in demand raises both price and quantity. An increase in supply lowers price but raises quantity. Do not mix them up.
## Elasticity
Price elasticity of demand (PED) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price, quoted without the minus sign.
| Value | Name | Price cut does this to revenue
| above 1 | elastic | raises total revenue
| exactly 1 | unitary | leaves revenue unchanged
| below 1 | inelastic | lowers total revenue
- Total outlay method: if spending moves the opposite way to price, demand is elastic; the same way, inelastic; unchanged, unitary.
- Demand is more elastic when there are close substitutes, the good is a luxury, it takes a large share of income, or buyers have time to adjust.

- A horizontal demand curve is perfectly elastic; a vertical one is perfectly inelastic. On a straight downward line, elasticity is 1 at the midpoint, above 1 on the upper half and below 1 on the lower half.
- Income elasticity: positive for normal goods (above 1 for luxuries), negative for inferior goods.
- Cross elasticity: positive for substitutes, negative for complements, zero for unrelated goods.
- Elasticity of supply: a vertical supply curve has elasticity zero; farm supply is inelastic in the short run.
> Price rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60; quantity falls from 400 to 300.
> PED = 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25, so demand is elastic.
! Put the quantity change on top. Dividing price change by quantity change gives the inverse (0.8 here), and it is always one of the options.
## Utility and consumer equilibrium

Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good. Marginal utility (MU) is the change in total utility (TU) from one more unit. The law of diminishing marginal utility says MU falls as more units are consumed. TU is at its maximum when MU is zero and falls once MU is negative.
With two or more goods, the law of equi-marginal utility says satisfaction is greatest when MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py and all income is spent. If one good gives more utility per rupee, buy more of it.
> MUx = 30, Px = Rs 10; MUy = 40, Py = Rs 20.
> MU per rupee: X gives 3, Y gives 2.
> Shift spending towards X until the ratios are equal.

Indifference curve approach (ordinal): an indifference curve joins combinations giving equal satisfaction. It slopes down and is convex to the origin because the marginal rate of substitution diminishes. Curves never cross. The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line touches the highest indifference curve.
## Consumer surplus
Consumer surplus = what a buyer is willing to pay − what she actually pays. Add the surplus on each unit bought.
> Willing to pay Rs 50, 40, 30, 20 for four units; price Rs 20.
! Do not confuse total willingness to pay (Rs 140) or total spending (Rs 80) with the surplus.
## Quick check
- Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, not the money price paid.
- Own price: movement along. Anything else: shift.
- PED above 1: cut price to raise revenue. PED below 1: raise price to raise revenue.
- Negative income elasticity means an inferior good; negative cross elasticity means complements.
- Consumer equilibrium: MU ÷ P equal for every good.
